segments.text: Database normalization, step by step. In this video, we'll take one messy table and turn it into a clean relational design.
Imagine a university that stores all its enrollments in one wide table.
The key is student ID plus course ID: one row per enrollment.
Look closer: Ana Ruiz twice, Databases three times, Computing five times.
That's redundancy, and it causes three anomalies.
First, the update anomaly. We rename course C10 in just one row, and now the same course has two different names.
Insert anomaly: course C30, Marketing, has no students yet. It can't be stored, because the key needs a student ID.
Delete anomaly: Ana drops Statistics. Deleting that one row also erases course C20 and the Maths department.
Normalization decomposes a table into smaller ones, guided by functional dependencies.
The goal: store each fact once.
The benefits: less redundancy, no anomalies, simpler updates, and less storage.
The costs: more tables and more joins, slower reads for some queries, and more design effort.
That's why some systems denormalize on purpose: for read-heavy analytics, it can be a sensible trade-off.
X determines Y means each value of X fixes exactly one Y.
Look at student S01. Both rows show the same name: Ana Ruiz.
The same goes for every student: student ID determines student name.
Student ID is the determinant, and student name is the dependent.
Counter-example: S01 got eight point five in one course, and seven in another.
So student ID alone doesn't determine grade: it needs the whole key.
Remember: dependencies come from what the data means, not from one sample of rows.
Enrollment has a composite key: student ID and course ID together.
Grade depends on the whole key. That's a full dependency.
Student name depends on student ID alone: a partial dependency.
The course and department columns depend on course ID alone.
Second normal form removes these partial dependencies.
Follow the chain: course ID, then department ID, then department name.
Department name describes the department, not the course.
It reaches the key only through department ID, which isn't a key attribute.
That's a transitive dependency, and third normal form removes it.
First normal form: one atomic value per cell. No lists.
Here, one cell holds two phone numbers. That breaks the rule.
We split it: one row per phone. Now every value is atomic.
Our Enrollment table already meets first normal form.
Second normal form: no non-key attribute may depend on just part of the key.
Student name depends on student ID alone, so it moves to a new Student table.
The course columns depend on course ID alone, so they move to a Course table, one row per course.
Enrollment keeps the full key and the grade. Its two key columns are now foreign keys.
Now each student, and each course, is stored exactly once.
New courses need no students, and renames touch one row.
Third normal form: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute.
In Course, department name depends on department ID, not directly on course ID.
It moves to a Department table keyed by department ID, which Course keeps as a foreign key.
Computing is now stored once, so renaming a department is a single update.
Four tables, each fact in one place: the design is in third normal form.
Boyce-Codd normal form is stricter: every determinant must be a candidate key.
Here, each teacher teaches one subject, so teacher determines subject.
But teacher isn't a candidate key: Professor Mora appears in two rows.
So we split: Teaches, with teacher and subject, and Tutoring, with student and teacher.
Now join the tables back on their keys,
and exactly the original six rows come back.
To recap: each normal form removes one kind of problem.
Each form builds on the previous one, up to Boyce-Codd.
Now practise it, in the Normalization section of the Databases practice site.
